_source.displaydescription:
Unlike many smaller bāhāḥs in Patan, Jom Bāhāḥ is neither a branch of any major bāhāḥ nor does it belong to the Vajrācāryas or Śākyas. It is a private Bāhāḥ of Śilpakāras (Lvahaṃkaḥmi), who are the stone workers. This Bāhāḥ is, in fact, an āgachẽ for the Śilpakāras. Therefore, they prefer to call it āgaṃchẽ, but not Bāhāḥ.

Locke (1985, 138-140) and Pruscha (1975, P-268) mention that this is called Jagata Kalyāṇa Vihāra in the Sanskrit language, however, the local residents argue that its Sanskrit name is Viśvakramā Avatāra Vihāra. A Yogāmbara statue is enshrined on the Bāhāḥ’s first floor inside the sacred and secret shrine (āgama). Those who are not initiated (dīkṣā) into the tradition are not allowed to enter the āgama. A large window capped by a toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya flanked by serpent girls is carved can be seen on the first floor.

The Bāhāḥ’s sanctum is on the ground floor where an idol of Akṣobhya has been enshrined as kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.[1] A stone Dharmadhātu Maṇdala[2] is erected in front of the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ. The door to the sanctum is flanked by Gaṇeśa, Candra, Mañjuśrī and Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara (to the right), and Mahākāla and Sūrya (to the left) and is capped by a stone toraṇa on which the images of Pañcabuddhas and Tārā have been carved. A stone statue of Nāmasaṃgīti is kept above the toraṇa. A Śikharakūṭa Caitya, two Dharmadhātu Maṇḍalas, and a statue of Śivapārvatī are established in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard.

The local residents believe that King of Patan, Siddhinarasiṃha Malla (r. 1620 – 1661) brought the Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas to Patan in order to make them construct temples and statues etc. in his kingdom. Sometime later, they (Śilpakāras and Sthāpitas) built two āgamas and started living permanently in Patan.

Locke (1985, 138) has mentioned a copper-plate inscription recording the date of the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction, however, no such inscription is in the Bāhāḥ at present. The earliest reference to this Bāhāḥ can be found on a palm-leaf manuscript from NS 778 (1658 CE).[3] Four Śākya clans (Khicā, Hvakhāḥ, Yākaḥ, and Katilāḥ Khalas) are the members of this Bāhāḥ. Previously, they used to perform the daily rituals turn by turn. However, at present, a Vajrācārya from Mikhā Bāhāḥ has been appointed for such rituals.[4] The Vajrācārya priest worships Yogāmbara enshrined in the āgama every year, on the 14th lunar day of the bright fortnight of Phāguna. Further, disipūjā is celebrated on the 11th of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa. Although this Bāhāḥ was initially built by the Śilpakāras, it is also shared by the Sthāpitas. Its digi, too, is divided into two parts. The western part of the Bāhāḥ belongs to the Sthāpitas and its eastern part to the Śilpakāras.

Footnotes

  1. ^ The Akṣobhya statue is dressed in a metal lhegā.
  2. ^ The date NS 795 (1675 CE) is inscribed on the Dharmadhātu (see the object LAL2680-011 below).
  3. ^ The manuscript records the name of a person (Siddhi Bhāro) who is a member of Oṃ (text: Jom) Bāhāḥ (cf. Rājavaṃśī 2041, 75).
  4. ^ He receives a monthly enumeration of 3500 rupees.

Guitaḥ Caitya 1 is located in the vicinity of the Mū Guitaḥ Bahī (LAL1980). It is built on a circular plan with four niches attached to the drum at each of the cardianal directions. Statues of the Four Buddhas have been placed in these niches. The main deity, Akṣobhya is placed in the southern niche with a lotus in front of him. The diameter of the single plinth drum is 670 cm, and the dome on of it has a diameter of  565 cm. Above the dome is a harmikā based on a square plan measuring 193 cm in width and 110 cm in height. There are thirteen steps or tiers above the harmikā and a ring of āmalaka around the central pillar (yaṣṭi). The finial is covered by a gilded parasol (chatra) with a pinnacle.

A date (NS 368) has been inscribed on the stone pedestal. For safety reason, the statue has been cased inside an iron fence. A stone mandaḥpāḥ lies on the ground in front of the statue. The image of Amitābha that was previously established inside the western niche was stolen in 1984, and a new image of the same deity was installed immediately after this. A statue of Amoghasiddhi is enshrined on the northern niche. The eastern niche of the Guitaḥ Caitya 1 houses a broken statue of Buddha, probably Ratnasambhava. Its right hand and its left thumb are both fragmented. L. Bangdel (1995, 229) has dated this statue back to ca. 13th century. The caitya is painted in white lime and its dome is topped with a harmikā upon which the vajradṛṣṭi eyes and ūrṇā have been painted. These paintings can be found on all four sides; they symbolise nobility and illumination.

Harṣa Bāhāḥ is a private Bāhāḥ built by Harṣanarasiṃha Śākya from Haḥkhā Ṭola, Patan in 978 NS (1858 CE). He was a saṅgha member of Kvāḥ Bāhāḥ, commonly known as Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra. He did not only built this Bāhāḥ, but also established an esoteric deity (āgamadevatā) and Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya in its premises. The house for the Bāhāḥ’s principal deity (kvāḥpāchẽ) has two stories and faces east.[1] The place for Bāḥā’s esoteric deity (āgama) and sanctum are located on its first[2] and second floor, respectively.  The door to the sanctum is crowned with a toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya (in the middle), and Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara (on the right and left) have been carved. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum as the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity (kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ).[3] Further, a Balabhadra statue made of stone is installed in front of the primary deity.

Jīvadhanasiṃha (probably a family member of Harṣanarasiṃha Śākya) offered a metal vajra to the Bāhāḥ in 984 NS (1864 CE). Harṣanarasiṃha also established a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala in the courtyard in 985 NS (1865 CE). The kvāḥpāchẽ was renovated in VS 2049 (1993 CE).

Harṣa Bāhāḥ is maintained and run by three families. Each saṅgha member from these three families is responsible to carry out the daily rituals for a month. The Bāhāḥ’s anniversary is on every tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha. On this day, the annual death rite (śrāddha) is also performed to commemorate the deceased elders (āḥju-aji).

Footnotes

  1. ^ Its roof is tiled with the jhĩgaṭī bricks, is capped by a caitya shaped pinnacle and is supported by the plain struts.
  2. ^ A trikhā window capped by a wooden toraṇa on which an image of Akṣobhya is carved, can be seen in this floor.
  3. ^ The statue faces east.

This Caitya is located to the south-west of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) of Bungmati. Bungamati is one of the oldest settlements in the Kathmandu Valley. This monument was constructed in the Licchavi period and stands testament to the antiquity of the settlement.  

The upper section of the Caitya was placed upon an unusually shaped brick and cement pedestal some time before 1990. Since then, the stone finial has separated from the structure and is now lying in pieces on top of the dome, which is also broken. The stone pavement around the Caitya was removed following the 2015 earthquake. The upper part of the Caitya has four small empty niches, each of which are surmounted by images of Kīrtimukha.

Locals worship the Caitya during their morning visit to the temples. Besides that, other regular worships are not observed at this Caitya.

_source.displaydescription: This caitya displays five layers of motifs (lotus, jewel, water, fire and thunderbolt) upon its upper part, and contains images of four Buddhas and four Tārās in the four cardinal directions and corners respectively. The seats of the deities are clad in brass, as are the toraṇa above them. These images are tied to iron rods to protect them against theft. The caitya's dome (garbha) and harmikā have been joined together using cement plaster, and the finial is already broken. Statues of the 13 donors are located on the southern face of vedikā alongside an inscription that records the construction date of the caitya.

This śikhara-styled Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira is located in the Bāghabhairava Temple complex (KIR0004). It has four doors, each crowned with a stone toraṇa, however, the sanctum is only accessible through the one which faces west. The remaining three which face east, north, and south, are false doors.[1] 

The temple is stone-built and stands on a two-layered plinth. The bell-shaped roof of the temple is capped by a jvālā nhyākaṃ, functioning as its pinnacle. The present stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara, consecrated inside the sanctum, was installed in 1984 CE after the old one was stolen (cf. Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057,43).

An inscription records that Siddhirāma Bhāro and his wife Gaṃgāmayi, residents of Kirtipur, built this temple and consecrated a stone statue of Bhavānīśaṅkara inside its sanctum in 1718 CE (NS 838).

A statue of this couple is installed in front of the temple. The inscription further mentions that they also established a guṭhī having endowed five ropanīs of land in order to maintain the temple and carry out the daily rituals. However, there is no information about the guṭhī and the land. Even the local community elders are not aware of any guṭhī or land related to this temple.

The priest of Bāghabhairava Temple performs the daily rituals. The Department of Archaeology cleaned and repaired the Bāghabhairava Temple complex in around 2007 CE including the Bhavānīśaṅkara Mandira.

Footnotes

  1. ^ The door in the north façade has an inscription recording the initial construction of the Temple. The second inscription found inside the sanctum is not related to this Temple.

Ī Bahī Vãtā Vihāra, also named Syõ Bahī ("ruined monastery"), is located to the north of Yampi Mahāvihāra in front of the northern Aśoka Stūpa. The courtyard with three shrines and three caityas is supposed to be a branch of the Yampi Mahāvihāra.

The Bahī area measures 21m x 30 m. The sunken courtyard is 82 cm below floor level, paved with flagstone tiles and measuring 10 m x 24 m. It is also home to three caityas. The southernmost Caitya is a vajradhātu caitya, while two other are śikharakūṭa caityas. To the east of the sunken courtyard, one can find three roofed shrines for the deities each Caitya facing west. The three structures are similar and measure 3.3 x 3.8 m. Local inhabitants worship these three small shrines as three different vihāras. Inside the shrines are three newly made stone images of Akṣobhya Buddha. 

Pruscha (1975, 209) and Locke (1985, 205)  wrote about this monument, and it seems that some remnants of the vihāra were still present at their time. However, there are some contradictions in their descriptions. Pruscha writes that bronze images of Dīpaṅkara were enshrined in the temple sanctum dated 1672 CE (NS 792). Locke states that "the northernmost shrine contains an image of Akṣobhya flanked by an image of Praj̃nāpāramitā on his right and one of Avalokiteśvara on his left; the central shrine has an image of Akṣobhya flanked by Padmapāṇi Lokeśvara on his right and Prajñāpāramitā on his left. The southern shrine has a headless image of Akṣobhya”.
_source.displayname: Ī Bahī Vãtā Vihāra (ca. 17th cent. CE) || ई बही वँता विहार || LAL1540
